chapters.title: Chapter 6: Taxes on Getting Money Out of the Company

lessons.title: Startup Tax Benefits: DPIIT Recognition, the Tax Holiday and the End of Angel Tax

body.text: Being called a startup gets you nothing from the tax department. Being recognised by DPIIT gets you some things. Getting the separate Inter-Ministerial Board certificate gets you the actual tax holiday, and fewer than two in a hundred recognised startups have one.

children.text: Founders routinely believe their company is exempt from tax for three years because someone said so at a demo day. The benefits are real but each has its own gate, and the gates are very different heights. This lesson separates what is easy to get, what is hard to get, and what everybody now gets automatically.

stats.label: DPIIT recognised startups
stats.context: Recognition is free, online, and comparatively easy to obtain

stats.label: With the tax holiday certificate
stats.context: Roughly 1.8% of recognised startups clear the second gate

stats.label: Turnover ceiling for the holiday
stats.context: Along with incorporation between 1 April 2016 and 31 March 2030

body.title: What each level of status actually gives you

columns.label: DPIIT recognition alone
points: Relaxed carry forward of losses through funding rounds under section 119 [old 78 and 79]
Eligibility to apply for the tax holiday, which is a separate process
Self-certification under several labour and environment laws
Relaxations in public procurement, and faster, cheaper intellectual property filings
No income tax exemption of any kind on its own

columns.label: DPIIT plus the Inter-Ministerial Board certificate
points: The full tax holiday under section 140 [old 80-IAC]
100% deduction of profits for three consecutive years
Chosen from the first ten years since incorporation
The ability to offer the ESOP perquisite deferral covered in the previous lesson
Granted to a small minority of applicants

body.caption: Conditions for the tax holiday under section 140 [old 80-IAC]

cells: A private limited company or an LLP
Between 1 April 2016 and 31 March 2030, after the sunset date was extended
Not exceeding ₹100 crore in the year the deduction is claimed
DPIIT recognition plus a certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board
The business must not be formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business, with limits on transferring used plant and machinery
100% of profits, for any three consecutive years chosen out of the first ten since incorporation

body.text: Read the last row carefully, because the choice is yours and it is worth money. Most startups lose money in their early years, when a 100% deduction of profits is worth exactly nothing. The holiday should be claimed in three consecutive profitable years, as late in the ten-year window as your growth allows, not in the first three years out of enthusiasm.

children.text: The Catch Nobody Mentions at Demo Day

A 100% deduction is not a 100% saving. Claiming the holiday means staying in the old regime, because the concessional 22% regime under section 200 [old 115BAA] surrenders exactly this kind of deduction. And a company in the old regime is inside minimum alternate tax, which sets a floor at 14% of book profit under section 206 [old 115JB]. A profitable startup with a tax holiday therefore pays MAT, not nothing.

body.title: Show me the math: what the holiday is really worth

children.text: A recognised startup with the certificate earns ₹2,00,00,000 of profit, which is also its book profit. Its turnover is under ₹400 crore, so its old-regime base rate is 25%, with 7% surcharge and 4% cess at this income level.

cells: Old regime with the section 140 holiday
Taxable income nil, so MAT applies at 14% of book profit plus surcharge and cess, an effective 15.5792%

children.text: So the holiday is worth having, but it reduces the effective rate to about 15.58% rather than to zero. It used to be better than this, because MAT paid during holiday years became credit that could be used later. Since the Finance Act, 2026 made MAT a final tax in the old regime, that credit no longer arises, which quietly reduced the value of every profit-linked holiday in the statute.

body.title: Try It: The Floor Under the Holiday
body.prompt: A startup claiming the section 140 holiday has book profit of ₹2,00,00,000 and taxable income of nil. Minimum alternate tax applies at an effective 15.5792%. What does it pay? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: ₹2,00,00,000 × 15.5792% is ₹31,15,840, or about ₹31.16 lakh. The effective rate comes from 14% of book profit, grossed up by 7% surcharge and 4% cess. A tax holiday removes the tax on taxable income, but MAT is computed on book profit, which the holiday does not touch.

children.text: Angel Tax: Gone, and Worth Understanding Anyway

For more than a decade, an unlisted Indian company that issued shares above what the tax department considered fair value was taxed on the excess as income. A startup raising at a valuation justified by ambition rather than assets could receive a demand on its own funding round. That provision is now history.

body.title: The rise and fall of angel tax

events.title: Introduced
events.description: A provision taxing share premium received by unlisted companies above fair market value, aimed at money being routed through inflated share issues.

events.title: Exemption framework for recognised startups
events.description: DPIIT-recognised startups could claim exemption subject to conditions and declarations, which helped some and created paperwork for everyone.

events.title: Extended to non-resident investors
events.description: The provision was widened to cover subscriptions from outside India, alarming foreign investors in Indian startups.

events.title: Abolished for everyone
events.description: The provision ceased to apply for all classes of investor, resident and non-resident, with no recognition or valuation conditions to satisfy.

body.text: Abolition works forward, not backward. Assessments and appeals for funding rounds raised before 1 April 2025 continue under the old law, and section 536 keeps those proceedings under the 1961 Act. If your company has an open angel tax matter from an earlier round, it does not disappear because the provision did. Valuation reports from those years should stay on file.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Benefit Needs Which Certificate?
body.question: A DPIIT-recognised startup without an Inter-Ministerial Board certificate is raising a round that will change its shareholding significantly. Which benefit can it rely on?
options: The 100% tax holiday on profits for three years
The relaxed carry forward of losses despite the change in shareholding
Deferral of ESOP perquisite tax for its employees
body.explanation: The carry forward relaxation under section 119 [old 78 and 79] runs off DPIIT recognition, so it is available. The tax holiday under section 140 [old 80-IAC] and the ESOP deferral both require the Inter-Ministerial Board certificate as well. Exemption from minimum alternate tax is not a startup benefit at all: it comes from being inside the section 200 regime, which a startup claiming the holiday cannot use.

children.text: The Full Picture for a Recognised Startup

body.caption: Every startup tax benefit in this course, and its gate

cells: 100% deduction of profits for three consecutive years out of ten
Losses survive a change in shareholding if all loss year shareholders continue to hold
Employees defer tax at exercise to the earliest of 48 months, sale or leaving
Share premium above fair value is no longer taxed as income
Nothing. It applies to every company and every investor
Extra 30% deduction on additional employee cost for three years
Nothing startup-specific, and it survives inside the 22% regime

body.label: The benefit most startups actually use
body.value: Loss carry forward, not the holiday
body.context: A company that loses money for six years and then turns profitable is protected mainly by its accumulated losses surviving funding rounds. That runs on DPIIT recognition alone, which is why recognition is worth obtaining even if the holiday never comes.

body.title: Scenario: Which Three Years?
body.scenario: A Pune software startup was incorporated in 2021 and holds both DPIIT recognition and the Inter-Ministerial Board certificate. It lost money until 2025, broke even in 2026, and expects profits of roughly ₹40 lakh in 2027, ₹1.5 crore in 2028, ₹4 crore in 2029 and ₹8 crore in 2030. It also carries ₹3 crore of brought forward losses from its early years.
body.prompt: When should it claim the three-year holiday, and what else must it weigh?
body.modelAnswer: Not yet, and the reason is that two reliefs are competing for the same profits. The brought forward losses of ₹3 crore will be set off first as profits arrive, which alone covers 2027 and most of 2028, so claiming the holiday in those years would waste it on income that was already sheltered. The ten-year window runs to 2031, and the holiday must be three consecutive years, which points towards 2029, 2030 and 2031, when profits are largest and the losses are exhausted. Three checks temper that. Turnover must stay within ₹100 crore in each year claimed, which a company growing this fast should model rather than assume. Minimum alternate tax will still apply at an effective 15.5792% of book profit during the holiday years, and since the Finance Act, 2026 that is a final tax with no credit, so the saving is the difference between the old-regime rate and the MAT floor, not the whole tax. And the company should compare that position against simply moving into the section 200 regime at 25.168% with no holiday, because if the holiday years are pushed too late or turnover breaches the ceiling, the concessional regime may be the better long-run home. The decision deserves a five-year model built with the accountant, since both the regime choice and the holiday years are effectively one-way doors.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Shape of the Holiday
body.textWithBlank: The section 140 [old 80-IAC] deduction covers 100% of profits for ___ consecutive years, chosen from the first ten years since incorporation.
body.explanation: Three consecutive years, and the choice of which three is yours. That makes the holiday a planning decision rather than an automatic benefit, and it is worth most when claimed in the company's strongest consecutive years within the ten-year window.

body.title: Getting and Keeping Startup Benefits
steps: Apply for DPIIT recognition early through the Startup India portal, since it is free and unlocks the loss carry forward relaxation
Apply separately to the Inter-Ministerial Board if you want the tax holiday or the ESOP deferral, and expect a far harder test
Keep a year-by-year projection of profits and turnover, so the three holiday years can be chosen deliberately
Track brought forward losses against projected profits, so the two reliefs do not overlap wastefully
Model the minimum alternate tax floor into every holiday year, and remember it now generates no credit
Make sure all loss year shareholders retain at least some shares through each funding round
Preserve valuation reports for pre-2025 funding rounds, since old angel tax matters continue under the 1961 Act
Re-check eligibility each year, particularly the ₹100 crore turnover ceiling

cards.definition: Registration as a startup with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, free and online, unlocking non-tax benefits and the loss carry forward relaxation.
The separate, much harder approval required for the tax holiday and the ESOP deferral.
The startup tax holiday: 100% deduction of profits for three consecutive years out of the first ten.
The former levy on share premium received above fair market value by unlisted companies, abolished from 1 April 2025 for all investors.
The last date of incorporation for eligibility, currently 31 March 2030 for the startup holiday.
Minimum alternate tax at 14% of book profit, which continues to apply during tax holiday years and now generates no credit.

points: DPIIT recognition and the tax holiday are two separate gates, and only about 1.8% of recognised startups clear the second

The section 140 [old 80-IAC] holiday gives 100% deduction of profits for three consecutive years out of the first ten, for companies incorporated between 1 April 2016 and 31 March 2030 with turnover within ₹100 crore
Claiming the holiday means staying in the old regime, so minimum alternate tax applies at an effective 15.5792% of book profit
Since MAT became a final tax, the holiday saves the gap between the old-regime rate and the MAT floor, not the whole tax
Choose the three holiday years deliberately, after brought forward losses are used and when profits are largest
Angel tax was abolished from 1 April 2025 for all investors, with no certificate or valuation condition required
Old angel tax assessments from earlier rounds continue under the 1961 Act, so keep those valuation reports

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Startup eligibility conditions, sunset dates and certification processes change, and the interaction between the holiday, minimum alternate tax and the concessional regime is fact-specific. Model your own position with a qualified chartered accountant before claiming any of these benefits.
